ZOOM OUT / THE MILKY WAY

Your cosmic address.

Earth → Solar system → Orion Spur → Milky Way → Local Group

A city of stars, seen from within.

Our galaxy has a central bar and sweeping spiral arms within a broad disk. The green marker in the model shows an approximate position for the Sun; individual points and arms are illustrative, not a measured star map.

A light-year measures distance: how far light travels in one year. Even light needs about 100,000 years to cross the Milky Way’s stellar disk.

THE OBSERVER'S NOTEBOOK

There’s always more
to look up to.

01 / WORLDS IN ORDER

One star. Eight very different worlds.

Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky planets. Beyond the asteroid belt lie the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn, then the ice giants Uranus and Neptune. Sizes and distances in this explorer are adjusted for visibility.

Explore NASA’s planet guide ↗
02 / BEYOND THE LIGHT

Where escape becomes impossible.

A black hole’s event horizon marks the boundary beyond which light cannot escape. The glowing material around some black holes is an accretion disk, heated as matter falls inward.

03 / THE STAR THAT POWERS OUR WORLD

The Sun: light from nuclear fusion.

Deep in the Sun’s core, hydrogen fuses into helium and releases energy. The visible surface is the photosphere; beyond it, the corona extends outward into space. The warm-colored model is an artistic illustration.

Sun facts · NASA ↗
04 / OUR CLOSEST COMPANION

The Moon: one world, changing phases.

The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight. Its phases change as we see different portions of its sunlit half during its orbit. It rotates once per orbit, so the same hemisphere faces Earth. Both its near and far sides experience daylight.

Moon facts · NASA ↗
